newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK budget fails to cool rate rise concerns.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK budget fails to cool rate rise concerns.

text.p: The pound scorched to a new five-year high against the mark, bonds slumped and shares fizzled after Labour's first budget in 18 years failed to erase speculation that British interest rates were heading higher.
"I will still be looking for a rate rise probably in August, possibly in July," said Mark Ramsden, economist at Stone and McCarthy in London.
Although Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown tightened the fiscal screws by more than anticipated, analysts said this may still not be enough to cool the sizzling British economy.

The pound bounced more than three pfennings higher against the mark from an earlier low to trade as high as 2.9193 marks. It was quoted at 2.9260/70 in late European trade compared with 2.9025/35 before the budget.
September gilt futures were down 22/32 at 113-30 in automated trade on LIFFE, compared with 114-27 before the budget.

The FTSE 100 share index ended 23.1 points or 0.49 percent higher at 4,751.4 but the September FTSE 100 futures contract was quoted 34 points down at 4,755 by 1630 GMT as further details of the budget were absorbed.

Brown, promising a budget that would deliver long term fiscal stability, said his measures would exercise a net fiscal tightening on the economy of 5.5 billion pounds ($9.1 billion) this year and 4.75 billion pounds next year.
Markets had been expecting a tightening of only around 4.0 billion pounds this year.

The highlight of his plan was a windfall tax on privatised utilities which would allow 3.25 billion pounds to be invested in a welfare-to-work programme, designed to get 250,000 young people off the dole.
But Mark Wall, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said overall, the cutbacks would not be enough.
"Strip out the windfall tax, which he said was included in the 5.5 billion stg figure, and the tightening will be two- to three-billion stg, which really isn't enough," he said.

Other highlights of the budget included a Public Sector Borrowing requirement (PSBR) forecast of 13.25 billion pounds for this year, also well below economists' forecasts for 16 billion pounds. In 1997/98, PSBR was forecast to shrink to 5.5 billion pounds.

As widely expected, Brown abolished tax credits for pension funds and companies and cut mortgage relief to 10 percent from 15 percent from 1998. He also raised stamp duty to 1.5 percent from one percent on property sales above 250,000 pounds and to two percent for sales above 500,000 pounds.
But he surprised markets by cutting the main corporation tax rate by two percent to 31 percent.
"The cut in the corporation tax was seen as very good news and it initially squeezed the market up, but then we got immediate abolition of dividend tax relief," said one share dealer.
Analysts said the main market reaction would come tomorrow, with most markets closing before the heart of the budget was released.
Overall though, the measures were not enough to curtail the high-spending British consumer.
"He has put a very light foot on the brakes, not enough to slow the economy quickly," Andrew Milligan, chief economist at General Accident in London.
